biggest_blockers.title: secret-iam-access
biggest_blockers.detail: The secret has grants for individual principals. Access on STACKIT Secrets Manager is coarser than a Secret Manager grant: a Secrets Manager user is read-only or read-write for the whole secrets engine of its instance, with no scope to one secret or path. Narrower access exists only as role bindings on the instance or on a secret group (a named list of secrets) in the alpha API of the service, and the pinned provider offers them as resources of its experimental IAM feature (stackit_secretsmanager_instance_role_binding_v1 and stackit_secretsmanager_secret_group_role_binding_v1), which its documentation says may change or be removed; the specification does not list the roles a secret group accepts. A grant of one Google principal on one secret therefore cannot be carried one to one: decide per principal whether it gets a user of the whole instance, a role binding on a secret group of the secrets it may read, or a separate Secrets Manager instance.
biggest_blockers.words: Decide how each principal with a grant on a secret reaches it on STACKIT

decision_register.basis: Records group four lists: the open decisions of the TargetPlans of the draft this run wrote, by the family of the producer (security group, routing, identity, logs, server) and the kind of the decision (plan decisions); the open critical semantics of the units, by the contract family and the semantic (critical semantics); the manual actions of the plans, by the family of the producer and the kind of the action (manual actions); and the open statements of the plans about units they write no resource for (a redesign, a review, a block, a failed model, or a step beside a unit whose draft a converter writes), by the family of the producer and the reason (plan statements). Plan decisions and manual actions cover only drafted units whose draft passed StackToIT's own checks, and only the families whose draft this run wrote from a plan: a family with no plan has none to list. A plan statement covers a unit the plan writes nothing for, whether or not a draft check ran over it; a statement that leaves nothing to a person (a unit the plan does not draft and no manual action of it names) is counted (closed_statements) and is no record. A record shows the review of an overlay beside the open state the engine reached; a review closes no critical semantic and changes no draft, target plan, gate, class, confidence or eligibility. An accepted plan decision frees the steps of the execution plan that wait for it only when the answer's effect acknowledges the current draft; an option that changes the draft keeps them held until the draft carries that option (the line of the option in decisions-template.yaml says whether an answer of the inputs file writes it or no answer of this build does). The one exception is an option that declines a default of the draft (choose-the-size, choose-the-snapshot-count, choose-the-zone-per-server, keep-the-source-rules-and-redesign-a-firewall, machine-type-with-a-local-disk, persistent-volume-for-the-data): the run that reads that answer writes its draft without the default, and the value the default stood for is yours to set. Records of the family "convert" are decisions of the converter's own generators, outside every plan: a CONSTRAINT_CONFLICT (a variable whose consumers' STACKIT bounds exclude one another keeps the source default) and an AMBIGUOUS_* selection (the source does not prove which instance, interface, key pair, gateway, peer, subnet, proxy, URL map or health check it means, so the draft holds a required variable without a default); the unit that owns one is not automation-eligible. They are listed for a drafted unit whose plan checks did not fail.

options.title: Replicate the data with the replication of the source engine until the cutover
options.effect: A person sets up the replication of the source engine so that the STACKIT instance follows the source while the application keeps writing to the source (for PostgreSQL, logical replication: the schema is copied first with pg_dump --schema-only, a publication on the source and a subscription on the target copy the existing rows and then the changes, and the sequences are copied inside the write freeze because they are not replicated). The source needs a change and a reboot to turn replication on, and the target must be able to reach the source. Inside the write freeze the person waits until the target has caught up, compares both sides and switches the clients, then removes the replication. For a PostgreSQL database the plan holds the steps of this option (the initial copy, the watch of the lag, the freeze, the final copy, the reconcile and the cleanup); for an S3 bucket this option is not available, because S3 Replication copies between Amazon S3 buckets and no STACKIT bucket is documented as a destination (the plan holds the two copy tools instead); for any other engine this option is not offered, because no STACKIT service other than PostgreSQL Flex documents the replication of a source engine into it (MariaDB, Key Value Store, OpenSearch and MongoDB Flex document none, and the SQLServer Flex page on transactional replication describes an on-premises publisher and does not name Amazon RDS as one), so the decision of such a store offers the export and the import with the engine clients where its service documents them, and the tool of the customer's own.

resolution_paths.title: Map the IAM roles of the service account to STACKIT roles: Bind a role of the STACKIT service account to the member
prerequisites: the Google roles granted on the service account and what each one allowed
the roles the authorization API lists for the STACKIT service account
effects: A role assignment on a STACKIT service account gives a role the authorization API lists for that account to a user, a service account or a client; given to a service account, it grants the Act-As permission, which lets that account impersonate the target account. A person re-maps each Google role on the account (using it, creating its keys, managing it) to a role of the STACKIT service account and binds it to the member. The assignment carries no condition and has no setting that removes the other holders of a role, so if the Google resource was authoritative (a binding for its role, a policy for the whole account) the replacing effect is not carried: a person lists who else holds a role on the account and removes what the source did not list. The resource is part of an experimental feature that is likely to change or be removed. The documents read do not state how a person, as opposed to a service account, acts as the account.
risk: A role chosen too wide lets a member act as the account more than the source allowed.

resolution_paths.title: Map the IAM roles of the service account to STACKIT roles: Bind a role of the STACKIT service account to the member
prerequisites: the Google roles granted on the service account and what each one allowed
the roles the authorization API lists for the STACKIT service account
effects: A role assignment on a STACKIT service account gives a role the authorization API lists for that account to a user, a service account or a client; given to a service account, it grants the Act-As permission, which lets that account impersonate the target account. A person re-maps each Google role on the account (using it, creating its keys, managing it) to a role of the STACKIT service account and binds it to the member. The assignment carries no condition and has no setting that removes the other holders of a role, so if the Google resource was authoritative (a binding for its role, a policy for the whole account) the replacing effect is not carried: a person lists who else holds a role on the account and removes what the source did not list. The resource is part of an experimental feature that is likely to change or be removed. The documents read do not state how a person, as opposed to a service account, acts as the account.
risk: A role chosen too wide lets a member act as the account more than the source allowed.

proposed.reason: Suggested from the workloads of the source, not confirmed by the customer: these groups are a reading of names, tags and references in the Terraform. Nothing is an application until the applications file (--applications) or the review file states it, and where it does the stated applications win and the suggestion is shown as a diff against them.
proposed.rule: One group per workload that is switched on: an ECS service, a Lambda function, a Kubernetes deployment, stateful set, daemon set, replication controller, pod, job or cron job, a load balancer with the instances and Auto Scaling groups it routes to, an instance or Auto Scaling group no load balancer fronts, or an EKS cluster when the estate holds no Kubernetes workload (such a group is a platform: its workloads are not visible in Terraform). A group holds its workload and the datastores, security groups, roles, log groups, secrets, keys and similar units that only that workload reaches: what the workload depends on (for an ECS service what its task definition names, for a Lambda function what its environment names, for a load balancer what it routes to), what those depend on in turn, the queues, streams, topics, buckets and EventBridge rules that feed a member (an event source mapping, a subscription, a rule target or the permission that names the rule, a bucket notification), the units a policy of a member names in a statement that is not a Deny, the units a DNS record that the workload names points at (a DNS record or a service-discovery registration that only points at a member is shown and adds no member), the datastore behind a security group whose ingress names a security group the workload itself uses, and the units that exist only for a member and depend on it (volumes, autoscaling targets, the secret of a database, the roles and node security group of a cluster, the Service, Ingress, autoscaler, network policy and disruption budget of a Kubernetes workload). An application tag the source states as a literal (Application, App, ApplicationName, AppName, ApplicationId, Workload, or Service where there is none of those) names the application: workloads that share the value are one group, a tagged unit no workload reaches joins the group of its value, and a unit tagged with another value than the group that reaches it is shared. A tag read from a variable is shown and never decides. A unit that more than one group reaches is shared and belongs to no group, unless exactly one of them carries the unit's tag value. The network, the ECS cluster and the gateways belong to no group, and a module name never makes one. A group is named by its application tag, else by the name of its workload, else by the family of its task definition, else by its address. For Google Cloud: a workload is a Cloud Run service, job or worker pool, a Cloud Function, a Compute Engine instance or managed instance group no load balancer fronts, the forwarding rule of a load balancer with the instances, groups and serverless services behind its backend services (the target proxy and the URL map are followed), or a GKE cluster when the estate holds no Kubernetes workload (a platform). A group holds the Cloud SQL, Memorystore, Spanner, Bigtable, Firestore, AlloyDB and Cloud Storage units, and the service accounts, secrets, keys, topics, queues, repositories, disks and addresses, that only the workload reaches: what its runtime configuration names (the environment and the secret mounts of a Cloud Run service or a Cloud Function), what those depend on in turn, and the resources an IAM role binding or member names together with the service account of a member (the role is not read, so it is a reference and not a stated grant). An application label the source states as a literal (application, app, workload, or service where there is none of those) names the application as a tag does; a label read from a variable is shown and never decides.

code_dependencies.rule: A code file belongs to an application when it sits under the common folder of that application's units (the folder of the files that declare them, relative to the source). The deepest such folder wins. A folder that two applications share, a file under no application's folder and an application whose units share no folder below the source root tie nothing: the hits of such a file are listed under the estate, and an application with no folder of its own reads the whole source and says so.

kubernetes_manifests.rule: A manifest object ties to a Terraform unit only when both state the same kind, the same name and the same namespace as literals (a kubernetes_* resource), or, for a Helm chart, when a helm_release names the chart by the literal local path of its folder. A name or namespace that is a variable, an expression or absent in the manifest ties nothing, and so does a namespace of the resource that is a variable or an expression; a kubernetes_* resource that states no namespace at all stands in the namespace default, which the hashicorp/kubernetes provider gives it, so only a manifest that states the namespace default ties to it. An object that more than one object or unit answers is not tied. A tie is evidence for the PROPOSED group that holds the unit (on every group that reaches a shared unit, labelled shared; on the tie itself when no group holds the unit) and never adds or removes a member. A Secret or ConfigMap that a manifest names and no manifest declares is resolved in Terraform only by the same literal name and namespace of exactly one kubernetes_secret or kubernetes_config_map.

legs.source: stackit-api-specifications services/postgres-flex/v3/postgres-flex.json (POST /v3/projects/{projectId}/regions/{region}/instances/{instanceId}/protections, operationId UpdateInstanceProtection, body isDeletable "Protect instance from deletion."; GetInstanceResponse.isDeletable; lines 4452-4455, 1088-1106, 1700-1704 of the mirror) and services/sqlserverflex/v3/sqlserverflex.json (same path); https://github.com/stackitcloud/stackit-api-specifications

https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/databases/postgresql-flex/how-tos/create-and-manage-instances-for-postgresql-flex/#instance-protection ("Instance Protection prevents an instance from being deleted. While it is active, deletion calls are rejected.") and the FAQ https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/databases/postgresql-flex/faq/ ("deleting an instance is immediate, permanent, and unrecoverable ... To prevent accidental deletion, enable Instance Protection."). The pages name the feature but not the tool that enables it: they do not state that Terraform supports it.

STACKIT provider schema 0.121.0 (the pinned provider version), re-read 2026-11-02: stackit_postgresflex_instance (attributes acl, backup_schedule, connection_info, encryption, flavor, flavor_id, id, instance_id, name, network, project_id, region, replicas, retention_days, storage, version) and stackit_sqlserverflex_instance (the same plus edition and options): no protection / deletable attribute, and no data source of the two services has one. The only attributes of the whole schema (resources and data sources) whose name contains protect, protection or deletable are protected (stackit_image, stackit_image_v2 and, new in 0.119.0, the results of the data source stackit_images: an image's protected flag), and protection (stackit_kms_key, stackit_kms_wrapping_key), all unrelated. The attribute sets of the two instance resources are the same as in the 0.116.0, 0.117.0 and 0.118.0 schemas (compared 2026-10-08 and 2026-10-10), and the STACKIT provider documentation of postgresflex_instance and sqlserverflex_instance (terraform-provider-stackit v0.116.0, local mirror) name no such attribute either. The fact holds on the pin: this refreshes the record of 2026-10-07, which cited the 0.117.0 schema and said that a 0.118.0 schema was not present, and was re-read on the 0.119.0 pin on 2026-10-10 (the 0.119.0 schema differs from 0.118.0 by two data sources and one resource description only) and again on the 0.120.0 pin on 2026-10-16 (the 0.120.0 schema differs from 0.119.0 by 17 block descriptions of the dremio, observability and secretsmanager services only, none of them a postgres/sqlserver flex type, an attribute or a type) and again on the 0.121.0 pin on 2026-11-02 (the 0.121.0 schema differs from 0.120.0 by one added attribute, config.cache_config of stackit_cdn_distribution, and one added data source, stackit_networks, found by a whole-tree comparison of the two files).

legs.source: STACKIT IaaS API v2 specification components.schemas.NIC.nicSecurity and CreateNicPayload.nicSecurity: "default": true, so a network interface created without nicSecurity has security (its security groups apply). NICSecurity: "If this is set to false, then no security groups will apply to this network interface."

https://docs.stackit.cloud/products/network/core-networking/network-interfaces/how-tos/create-and-manage-network-interfaces/ ("the optional flag `--nic-security` enables you to turn network interface security on. Per default it is disabled."), read 2026-10-08 through a page-summarising fetch tool. The sentence is about the CLI flag, not the API, so the two may both be true (the CLI would then send an explicit false); the page does not say. Probe 11: the page sentence is not true of STACKIT CLI 0.73.0 (its own help says "--nic-security ... (default true)", and `network-interface create` without the flag stored nicSecurity true), so the page is the outlier, not the specification.

STACKIT provider schema 0.121.0 resource_schemas.stackit_network_interface.block.attributes.security: optional, computed bool without a stated default; the provider (mirror tag v0.116.0, networkinterface/resource.go:643) sends nothing when it is unset, so the API default decides. Probe 11 (provider 0.118.0): a network interface written without security was stored and read back with nicSecurity true (state security = true). The attribute is the same in the 0.119.0 schema (re-read 2026-10-10) the 0.120.0 schema (re-read 2026-10-16) and the 0.121.0 schema (re-read 2026-11-02).

groups.message: This trigger starts its builds on a Pub/Sub message. The replacement workflow lists the events that start it in its own on: section; the pages of STACKIT read describe pipelines that run whenever changes are pushed to a repository, so a pull request, a schedule or a manual start is verified by a person against the Forgejo Actions reference.

A container mounts a Cloud SQL connection, a Cloud Storage bucket (through Cloud Storage FUSE) or an NFS share. The draft writes no volume for these and holds the pods until a person decides: connect to the migrated database or object store over the network instead of the mount, or mount a share or a volume of the cluster yourself.
The account ID is not visible statically; the STACKIT account is named after the source address. — a variable's default, not a fact

The secret has grants for individual principals. Access on STACKIT Secrets Manager is coarser than a Secret Manager grant: a Secrets Manager user is read-only or read-write for the whole secrets engine of its instance, with no scope to one secret or path. Narrower access exists only as role bindings on the instance or on a secret group (a named list of secrets) in the alpha API of the service, and the pinned provider offers them as resources of its experimental IAM feature (stackit_secretsmanager_instance_role_binding_v1 and stackit_secretsmanager_secret_group_role_binding_v1), which its documentation says may change or be removed; the specification does not list the roles a secret group accepts. A grant of one Google principal on one secret therefore cannot be carried one to one: decide per principal whether it gets a user of the whole instance, a role binding on a secret group of the secrets it may read, or a separate Secrets Manager instance.

evidence_refs name rows of evidence_ledger. Evidence that names a record internal to the product is not listed, and evidence that states no check date and no date to check it again is listed UNDATED, never CURRENT.

price_snapshot.statement: These are list prices only: no quantity is read and no total is built from them here; the quantities, amounts and totals of the priced families are in financial/cost-model.json, which computes a usage or an egress only where the assumption file states it. This block names the snapshot of the public STACKIT price list the run cites and, for each drafted resource of a kind the price rules list, the list price of the one SKU a tested rule joins it to, or why it has none.
limits: A list price is the price of one unit of one SKU. It is not a cost: this block reads no quantity and builds no total; the quantities, amounts and totals of the priced families are in financial/cost-model.json.

A resource is joined to a SKU only where the draft itself names the machine type, performance class or flavor; where the draft leaves that to a person (a variable), no SKU is named and the resource is NOT_ASSESSED.

Prices are net list prices of the public STACKIT price list: excluding taxes, with no contract discount, no savings plan and no other currency. A SKU that is not in the public list, a deprecated SKU and the metro variant of a SKU are never used as a price.
Egress and traffic, support plans, the container registry and every resource of a kind the price rules do not list have no row: nothing is stated about their cost.
Only the region eu01 is looked at: it is the region of the knowledge-base catalogue the draft takes its flavors from.
The row of a volume is the per-hour fee of its performance class; the capacity fee of the disk is a separate SKU that depends on the size, and is a line of the cost model, not a row here.

cost_model.statement: An initial infrastructure cost estimate under explicit assumptions (the scenario and the assumption file this model names), not a bill: list prices (net, no discount, no Spot, no savings plan, no private price) times quantities the source or the assumption file states. A total is FULL only when every line of its scope is priced; a line that cannot be priced says why and is never filled in, and an unknown quantity is neither 0 nor 1. A savings percentage is given only for the same scope, in one currency (or with an exchange rate that names its source and date), with every line of both sides priced. No usage, traffic, request or egress cost is computed unless the assumption file states the use of one month: a line priced on a stated use is an assumption and says so, and without it the line has its price and no amount. No support, licence, operations or migration labour cost is computed. The one one-off item the model states is what both estates cost while they run side by side during the cutover (parallel_run_months of the assumption file): it is stated apart and is in no total, comparison or saving.

limits: Only EC2 instances (aws_instance), EBS volumes (aws_ebs_volume and the root and block devices of an instance), RDS for PostgreSQL instances (aws_db_instance: instance hours, allocated storage, provisioned iops, gp3 throughput), Amazon Aurora (aws_rds_cluster_instance: the instance hours; aws_rds_cluster: the consumed storage and the I/O requests with their price and no quantity) the network families (aws_nat_gateway, aws_lb, aws_eip and the public address an instance asks for, aws_route53_zone, aws_internet_gateway: see the line on the network families below) and the managed-service families (aws_ecs_service on Fargate, aws_mq_broker, aws_elasticache_replication_group and aws_elasticache_cluster, aws_opensearch_domain, aws_dynamodb_table: see the line on them below), the control plane of an Amazon EKS cluster (aws_eks_cluster), the nodes of its managed node groups (aws_eks_node_group) and the storage of S3 buckets and EFS file systems (aws_s3_bucket, aws_efs_file_system: see the line on them below) have lines on the source side, and only STACKIT servers (each with its boot volume), volumes, PostgreSQL Flex instances (flavor, storage class, storage capacity), public IPs, load balancers, DNS zones, RabbitMQ, Valkey, OpenSearch and MariaDB instances (their plan), MongoDB Flex instances (their flavor), SKE clusters (the cluster hour and each node pool), KMS keys, Secrets Manager and Logs instances on the target side; the other drafted resources have a line that says they have no quantity rule, and every other source resource has no line and is listed in the out-of-model group.

The network families have a line on each side, never a total over a partial set. NAT gateway: the hour of a zonal public NAT gateway is priced and the data it processes has the per-GB price and no quantity; the STACKIT price list holds no SKU for a NAT gateway or for outbound address translation, so its target line is PRICE_NOT_FOUND (a service the list does not price is not free). Load balancer: the hour of an Application or Network Load Balancer is priced and its capacity units have the price and no quantity; the target line is the hour of the plan (plan_id; a Network Load Balancer that states none is read as the default p10 the provider documents). Public IPv4 address: the hour of an Elastic IP, and of the address an instance asks for with associate_public_ip_address = true (not an address its subnet or launch template decides), against the hour of a stackit_public_ip. DNS: the month of a hosted zone (the first tier of the Route 53 price; the tier is the account's) and its queries (no quantity); the STACKIT list prices a zone by the number of records it may hold, which the draft does not state, so its target line is AMBIGUOUS. Data transfer out: the per-GB price of the first tier (every tier is named on the line) on the line of the internet gateway and no quantity; the STACKIT list holds no SKU for it, so its target line is PRICE_NOT_FOUND. A quantity that is a measurement of use (GB, capacity unit hours, queries) is never in a Terraform source and is never made up: such a line has its price and no amount. The prices are the On-Demand rows of the AmazonEC2 (NAT gateway, load balancers), AmazonVPC (public IPv4), AWSDataTransfer and AmazonRoute53 offers of the price cache, which `stacktoit prices refresh --provider aws --region R` fetches (`--offer` names one); a line whose offer the cache does not hold names the offer and the command.

The managed-service families are priced from the On-Demand rows of the AmazonECS (Fargate vCPU and GB hours: the cpu and memory of the task definition times the desired count, which is never taken as zero when it is not stated), AmazonMQ (broker hour by engine, instance type and deployment mode; its storage has the price and no quantity), AmazonElastiCache (node hour by engine and node type times the nodes of a replication group), AmazonES (data and dedicated master node hours, EBS GB-month) and AmazonDynamoDB (provisioned read and write capacity unit hours when the table states them, at the rate beyond the free first tier, which is the whole account's; request units and storage have the price and no quantity) offers, which `stacktoit prices refresh --provider aws --region R` fetches (`--offer` names one); Fargate Spot, ECS on EC2 capacity, Windows tasks, global datastores and non-standard table classes are out of the model. The control plane of an Amazon EKS cluster is the cluster hour of the AmazonEKS offer (the standard-support hour: a cluster of a Kubernetes version past standard support is billed the extended-support hour in addition, which is not in the line, and the line says so; a local cluster on AWS Outposts and a Provisioned Control Plane tier are out of the model; the management fee of EKS Auto Mode is said, not computed). A managed node group costs nothing of its own (Amazon EKS User Guide, Managed node groups): its line is the EC2 hour of the first of its instance_types, or of its launch template, or the t3.medium Amazon EKS uses when none is stated, times its desired_size, with the operating system, tenancy and purchasing option rules of an instance (a Spot or Windows node group is not priced as On-Demand Linux) and the EBS volumes its launch template maps as lines of their own; the root volume of the nodes is not in it. The storage of an S3 bucket (S3 Standard, tiered by the size stored in a month) and of an EFS file system (Standard, or One Zone when availability_zone_name is stated) has its price and no quantity, because the data held is a measurement of use that no Terraform source states: the line names the entry of the assumption file that would price it (variable volume_size, unit GB), and the other storage classes, the requests, the transfer and the throughput are not in it. On the target side a RabbitMQ, Valkey (Key Value Store), OpenSearch or MariaDB instance is the hour of the SKU of its plan_name (the SKU is named by the plan, INFERRED from the names of the list, and its nodes and disk are checked against the list's attributes); a plan the draft leaves to a person is TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN. An SKE cluster is the cluster hour, and each node pool it states is a line of its own: the server flavor hours of its machine_type (the join of a server) times its nodes, the range between its minimum and its maximum when they differ, an unknown quantity with the price when the draft states either as a variable, and TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN when the machine type is a variable; the boot volume of each node is not in the line, and the machines of a pool are never set against the source lines of the nodes of an EKS node group (a unit of its own) or of an ECS cluster's capacity, so a pool is a target-only line (see below); the cluster hour of an SKE cluster stands against the control plane hour of an EKS cluster, but a unit whose item holds a target-only pool is not computed, so no saving is stated over it. A MongoDB Flex instance is the hour of the SKU MongoDB-Flex-<cpu>.<ram>-<Single|Replica|Sharded> of its flavor.cpu, flavor.ram and options.type (INFERRED from the names of the list, and checked against the SKU's own attributes; the rate of a Replica SKU is read as that of the whole instance with its nodes); a flavor a person sets is TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN, a flavor the list has no SKU of is PRICE_NOT_FOUND, its storage and backups are not computed, and because this build prices no DocumentDB cluster on the source side its line is target only (see below). A software KMS key version and a GB of log ingestion have their list price and no quantity; Secrets Manager is AMBIGUOUS between its tiers (the number of secret versions). A priced target line of a family whose source side has no line for the unit (an SKE cluster and its node pools, a MariaDB instance, a MongoDB Flex instance, a RabbitMQ plan against a source with no priced broker) is target only: it is counted in the STACKIT total, listed apart with its amount (target_only on the line and target_only_lines, target_only_min and target_only_max on the total), and kept out of every comparison and every saving, because no source amount stands against it; each comparison states the lines and the amount it leaves out, on both sides.

The instance hours and the allocated storage of an RDS for PostgreSQL instance are priced from the AmazonRDS offer of the price cache (On-Demand list prices, Single-AZ or Multi-AZ as the source states; `stacktoit prices refresh --provider aws` fetches it with the AmazonEC2 offer); its provisioned IOPS (io1, io2, gp3) and the provisioned throughput of gp3 storage come from the same offer, gp3 only above the performance its allocated storage includes (a baseline of 12,000 IOPS and 500 MiB/s from 400 GiB, nothing more can be provisioned below it: Amazon RDS User Guide, DB instance storage); without that offer the lines are PRICE_SOURCE_ABSENT and the instance is never in the computed subtotal. An Aurora instance (engine aurora-mysql or aurora-postgresql) is the instance hour of its engine, its instance class and the storage configuration of its cluster, from the same offer (rules version 3 of its narrowing): Aurora Standard when the cluster states no storage_type (the provider's documented default), Aurora I/O-Optimized for storage_type = "aurora-iopt1", and both prices open (AMBIGUOUS) when the source does not state it as a fact or the instance's cluster is not a resource of the source; the cluster's consumed storage (a GB-month) and, on Standard, its I/O requests are measurements of use and have their price and no quantity. An Aurora Serverless v2 instance (db.serverless), an instance of a Multi-AZ DB cluster, backup storage beyond the free allocation, Global Database and the Data API are not computed. An offer narrowed before the Aurora rows were kept answers PRICE_SOURCE_ABSENT with the refresh command on each Aurora line. A PostgreSQL Flex Replica flavor is priced once per instance: the list gives its SKU 3 nodes and a higher rate than the Single SKU (1.6 to 2.0 times it, never 3 times), and the rate is read as that of the whole instance (evidence class INFERRED from the price list; each such line says so); how much of its storage is billed (once or per node) the list does not say, so its storage lines have the SKU and no quantity.

The PostgreSQL Flex storage class premium-perf<n>-stackit is priced as the SKU "Block Storage for PostgreSQL Premium-Performance <n>" per disk and its capacity as "Block Storage for PostgreSQL Premium-Capacity" per GB (evidence class INFERRED from the names of the price list; each such line says so). For a replica flavor the list gives the storage per node and does not say whether the booked size is billed once or for each node, so its disks and gigabytes are the range between the two readings. The IOPS and throughput shown for the class in the technical mapping are the attributes maxIOPerSec and maxTroughInMB of that performance SKU in the price list (the catalogue states none for a PostgreSQL Flex class); whether the class covers what the source provisions is a comparison of those figures, not a statement that the two perform alike.

The lines fall into three groups: the computed subtotal (only the source units every line of which is priced on both sides, so both subtotals cover the same units), the lines whose price is known and whose quantity is not (the quantity that is needed is named), and what is not computed (a unit of a type out of the model, a unit with no line on one side, or a line without a price), listed by resource and never zero.

Source prices are the On-Demand list prices of the AWS offer file in the price cache (USD, net, region of the resource); Spot, Reserved, Savings Plans, Dedicated Host, capacity reservation and private prices are never used. The operating system and licence come from the assumption file: the source does not state them.

The offer file bills an EBS volume per GB-month; this build reads it as GiB-month, the unit a volume is sized in: the Amazon EBS pricing page states "on this page, GB = 1024^3 bytes" (OFFICIAL_DOCUMENTED for that page; applying it to the offer file's unit is INFERRED). The IOPS and throughput of a gp3 volume are priced only above the baseline included in the price of its storage (3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s: Amazon EBS User Guide, OFFICIAL_DOCUMENTED), per volume; io2 IOPS are priced in tiers whose edges the offer file carries in descriptions only, and are not priced.

Target prices are the net EUR list prices of the public STACKIT price list in the price cache (region eu01). A machine type or performance class the draft leaves to a person is TARGET_NOT_CHOSEN; the metro variant of a SKU is never substituted.
The target capacity price of a volume is the capacity SKU of its performance class's tier (evidence class INFERRED from the structure of the price list).

One month is the 730 hours of the scenario; a per-month rate is applied as the file gives it. Snapshots, backups, support plans and every other cost of usage, traffic or requests that this build has no line for are not computed.
A saving is compared only for the same source units on both sides and in one currency (an exchange rate from the assumption file, with its source and date, converts one side).

Google Cloud source lines are priced from the On-Demand list prices of the Cloud Billing Catalog API in the price cache (USD, net, the region of the resource; `stacktoit prices refresh --provider gcp --region R`, with your own API key in STACKTOIT_GCP_BILLING_API_KEY, fetches them; `--offer` names one catalog). The catalog has no machine-type or disk-type field: each line joins its SKU by the words of the SKU's description and needs exactly one SKU to fit (a join INFERRED from the descriptions, said on each line); no fit is PRICE_NOT_FOUND and more than one is AMBIGUOUS, never a pick.

What the Google Cloud model prices: google_compute_instance and google_compute_instance_from_template (a predefined or custom machine type as its vCPU hours and its memory hours, a shared-core type as its instance hour; the GPUs, the Local SSD, the boot disk with its Hyperdisk or extreme-disk IOPS and throughput; the external address an access_config asks for), google_compute_instance_group_manager and google_compute_region_instance_group_manager (the instances of the one instance template the group names, between the bounds of the autoscaler that targets it, else target_size), google_compute_disk and google_compute_region_disk, google_compute_address (external), google_sql_database_instance (PostgreSQL, MySQL and SQL Server: vCPUs, memory, storage and, for SQL Server, the edition licence; Enterprise Plus, shared-core and legacy named tiers), google_container_cluster and google_container_node_pool, google_redis_instance, google_storage_bucket (also dual-region), google_compute_router_nat, google_dns_managed_zone, google_pubsub_topic, and the serverless, data, security, network and data-processing services: Cloud Run services and jobs, Cloud Functions, BigQuery, Spanner, Bigtable, Firestore, Filestore, Secret Manager, Cloud KMS, Cloud Logging, Cloud Tasks, Cloud Scheduler, Artifact Registry, Dataproc, Dataflow, Composer, load balancer forwarding rules, Cloud Armor, VPN tunnels and Interconnect (the coverage file of this run lists each line). Every other Google Cloud resource has no line and is listed in the out-of-model group.

A machine series whose memory per vCPU this build does not read from the documentation, a Cloud SQL tier of another series, a Spanner or Firestore multi-region, a custom dual-region bucket and a Composer 1 environment are out of the model or KEY_NOT_READ with the reason on the line; a forwarding rule is priced as an additional rule, without the minimum charge that covers the first rules of a project. Spot, preemptible, sole-tenant, flex-start and reservation-bound capacity is never priced as On-Demand. A premium operating system image (Windows Server, SQL Server, Red Hat or SUSE Enterprise Linux, Ubuntu Pro) gets a licence line that names the licence and is PRICE_NOT_FOUND, so the instance is never in a computed subtotal without its licence fee; an image the source does not state is read as one with no licence fee and the line says so (an ASSUMPTION).

No discount is applied: the sustained-use discount of the N1, N2, N2D and C2 families, committed-use discounts, the free tier of the billing account (one zonal or Autopilot GKE cluster, the first gigabytes of Pub/Sub) and negotiated prices are not in a list price. A quantity that is a measurement of use (the data a bucket holds, the data a NAT gateway or a topic moves, the VMs a NAT gateway serves, the requests and the instance time of a Cloud Run service or function, the bytes a BigQuery query scans, the operations of a key, a secret or a database, the log volume, the worker hours of a Dataflow job) is never in a Terraform source: such a line has its price and no quantity, until the assumption file states the use. A node count of a regional GKE cluster that lists no node_locations is not known (the zones GKE chooses are not in the source), so its nodes are not priced.

fields.closes_when: the measured amount and the date of the measurement are recorded
fields.words: copy volume: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (the amount of data of {subject} to copy: the used space measured on the source; the provisioned capacity of the source is not the amount of data; closed when the measured amount and the date of the measurement are recorded)

fields.closes_when: the rate measured over a representative period is recorded, with the time a final pass needs at that rate
fields.words: change rate: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (how much data the writers of {subject} change per hour; closed when the rate measured over a representative period is recorded, with the time a final pass needs at that rate)

fields.closes_when: the owner of the application agrees the start and the end of the window and it is recorded
fields.words: write-freeze window: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (the window in which the writers of {subject} stop for the final pass; closed when the owner of the application agrees the start and the end of the window and it is recorded)

fields.closes_when: the time of the final pass and the result of its checks are recorded
fields.words: last sync: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (the time the final pass ends and its checks hold; closed when the time of the final pass and the result of its checks are recorded)

fields.closes_when: the return point is recorded with its time and how it is restored
fields.words: return point: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (the state of {subject} the migration returns to on a rollback: the source as it was at the write freeze, or a named snapshot or backup; closed when the return point is recorded with its time and how it is restored)

fields.closes_when: the method is agreed and its result after the final pass is recorded
fields.words: consistency check: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (how the copy of {subject} is shown complete and unchanged after the final pass: the used space and a checksum of the data (of the files, or the row counts of the tables) agree with the source; closed when the method is agreed and its result after the final pass is recorded)

fields.closes_when: the test passes on the target and its result is recorded
fields.words: validation on the target: UNKNOWN — supplied by Migration Owner (the test the application that uses {subject} passes on STACKIT with the copied data before the cutover, agreed with the owner of the application; closed when the test passes on the target and its result is recorded)

fields.closes_when: the date until which {subject} is kept is recorded
fields.words: source retention: UNKNOWN — supplied by Migration Owner ({subject} is not retired until the owner decides to retire it; how long it and its final backup are kept after that is the owner's; closed when the date until which {subject} is kept is recorded)

fields.closes_when: the criteria (which check fails, which metric passes which limit, by when) are recorded before the cutover
fields.words: rollback trigger: UNKNOWN — supplied by Migration Owner (the owner's decision to go back; the criteria that call it; closed when the criteria (which check fails, which metric passes which limit, by when) are recorded before the cutover)

fields.closes_when: the choice is recorded before the cutover
fields.words: data written to the target: UNKNOWN — supplied by Data Architect (what is written on STACKIT after the switch is not in Google Cloud: it is copied back to {subject} before Google Cloud serves again, or accepted as lost; closed when the choice is recorded before the cutover)

machine_files.description: The full assessment: every unit, finding and count, machine-readable. Every number in this workspace is read from it.
The assessment in words: the run status and its checks, and for each unit the class, the confidence and the STACKIT target proposed.
The working behind engineering/architect-report.md: the relations and combinations the engine evaluated for the decisions that depend on them. Nothing here is a second decision.
The source and the target architecture as a diagram in Mermaid text, for tools that draw it. The Architecture section of this page draws the same units itself.
A draft order of work: waves computed from the dependencies between units. A starting point for the architect's plan, not a schedule.
One row per unit for spreadsheet review.
One row per dependency between units, for the architect to confirm, correct or complete.
The compact model the pages show, machine-readable. No page embeds it: the pages are complete without it, and a tool reads the model from this file.
The front page: the header, the navigation and the Overview. The other sections are the pages in pages/.
The Applications section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Which application each unit belongs to, and each application's migration strategy.
The Architecture section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The units of the estate and what the assessment decided for each.
The Decisions section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The decisions people must take, aggregated, with their options, owners and deadlines.

The Target Fit section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. How well each STACKIT target fits: service, interface, Terraform, region, maturity, quota, lifecycle, operability, support and security.
The Migration Plan section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Waves, prerequisites, data movement and the order of work.

The Security & Resilience section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. What has been proven about security and resilience, what has not, and what needs evidence from outside; the resilience of each unit, where this run assesses it, is on the Operations page.
The Sovereignty section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Dependencies, jurisdiction, data placement, key control and exit paths, source against target.
The Operations section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Whether the target can be run: identity, audit, observability, backup, restore, support and lifecycle.
The Costs section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Priced and unpriced coverage, and the inputs a cost estimate needs.
The Evidence section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The counts, versions and sources behind every statement in this workspace.
The Engineering Evidence section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. The machine-readable files and the Terraform draft.

The Work Board section as a page of its own, with the same header and navigation. Every job of the migration in one list, in four queues: who does it, what it waits for, what closes it and which file it carries out.
The decision register, machine-readable, with a template of the decisions file to fill in.
The decision records as rows for a spreadsheet.
The decision records in words.

The five-minute answer as a document: the run summary, what holds the estate back, what people must decide, the shape of the target and what has and has not been established. It restates numbers this file holds and scores nothing.

One row per application of the applications file you gave, with the values as you wrote them (a value you did not write is marked not provided), and one row per unit claimed by several applications. Header only without an applications file.

The dependency order of the units, one row per unit: the wave, WITHHELD when a part of the source was not read in full, or REFUSED for a unit the partial draft refuses for a missing input (in no wave). An order of work, not a schedule.

The register of what a person has to do, decide or establish before the draft is deployed, one typed row per item: gaps in the reading of the source, critical semantics left open, open decisions and manual actions of the plans, workload items that wait for evidence, and validation rows not yet established. Every member of decisions.json is a row; each row names the decision record that holds it. It lists what is open and decides nothing.

The Work Board as a sheet: one row per job of the migration, in one of four queues (provide information, approve a design, perform migration work, verify), with its owner, priority, what it waits for, what closes it, its evidence, the files it carries out and the steps of the execution plan it holds. Every step of the plan is in exactly one job, or listed as not taken; pages/work-board.html shows the same jobs. The rows are in board order (queue by queue); the order to work in is the order of migration/work-items.json and the Start here list of the page. Header only when the run wrote no execution plan.

The jobs of the Work Board as data, with the run they belong to: each job's id, kind, queue, owner, state, what it waits for, what closes it, its files and steps and, for a decision, its options and how each is carried out, and the one order in which the report names the jobs (the first job, then the jobs that can start, then the others). It is the file the guided work command reads; it states no state or priority of its own, and a job it lists is not done.

Each source unit beside its STACKIT target, one row per unit (the standing column says what the knowledge base and the run state of the unit's target; the drafted and manual counts of the console and of the draft's README partition what the draft did, and are another count): the target service and its resources (the knowledge base's candidate resource types), the resource types the draft really writes for the unit (drafted_resources: empty when it writes none, marked not assessed when no draft was read), or in words that there is no target, that the unit is refused or that the source switches it off, and how many of its settings are kept (PRESERVED), changed (TRANSFORMED), accepted (ACCEPTED_*) or still to do (everything else, including anything not known). Counted from the rows of assurance/equivalence-ledger.csv; a unit with no ledger row has four zeros, which says nothing was counted, not that nothing is left to do. Header only when the Workspace holds no counts.

The drill-down from each application of the customer's file and each group the run suggested (PROPOSED: a reading of the source, not confirmed by anyone), one row per member unit: the Google Cloud resource, the STACKIT target in the words of migration/source-target.csv, the ids of the decisions that still ask something about the unit, the steps of the execution plan that carry it with the number an answer leaves not taken, the Kubernetes manifest objects that tie to it by an exact literal match, and what the code scan says of the application. A run that read no plan or built no register marks those cells as not assessed, which is not an empty list. Header only when the Workspace holds none.
For each unit, the open decisions and manual actions that stand between its draft and its deployment, as its plan states them.

One row per stateful source unit (a database, a cache, a volume, a file share, an object store): its source and target service, the data class, RPO and downtime tolerance you stated (or marked not provided), the provisioned capacity the source states (not the size of the data) and the cutover dependency. The mechanism of every unit is UNKNOWN: StackToIT never moves data.
The same units in words, with what the source and the plans do and do not state about each. No size, change rate, duration, transfer rate or downtime is ever stated, and no mechanism is chosen.

The data_movement block of workspace.json with every stateful source unit (the facets, the unknowns, the provisioned capacity and where each fact is read from), as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to. workspace.json carries the tally of the units.
The units of the estate and the dependencies among them as a Mermaid flowchart, with the units of each application drawn together.
The same units with the STACKIT service proposed for each, its class and confidence, as a Mermaid flowchart.
The same units with what the move changes for each: its class, whether it has a target, and how many properties the draft names as not carried.
The drawing of the source architecture of the Architecture section, as a file of its own, without the links of the page.
The drawing of the proposed STACKIT target of the Architecture section, as a file of its own.
The drawing of what the move changes, as a file of its own.
What has and has not been established about the draft, row by row, with the global invariants. It approves nothing and asserts neither equivalence nor that the draft is safe to apply.
How much of the source was read, the source providers the assessment saw and the source types the knowledge base does not know.
How the STACKIT targets of the units stand in the capability catalogue and in the pinned provider (maturity, lifecycle), and the readiness dimensions.
The workload readiness of the units (installation, source artifacts, target preconditions, cutover, day 2) and the support options STACKIT evidences. Terraform generated is not workload ready.
For each STACKIT service of the draft and each framework in scope, the state of the provider's own evidence. It says nothing about the compliance of your workload.
The cells of compliance-evidence.md as rows for a spreadsheet.

The equivalence ledger: one row per unit and semantic of the assessment that the source states (workspace.json counts those it does not state), and one row per unit and property for the properties the draft does not carry, no semantic accounts for or that are critical and still open. Each row says how the source states the value, what proves the disposition, where the draft carries it and what stays open. Dispositions are the words the assessment uses today; PRESERVED appears only where the assessment or the draft's plan states it.

The evidence the ledger and the other blocks cite, one row per document, with what it backs, the date it was checked, the date after which it is to be checked again and its state. Evidence that states no such dates is UNDATED, never CURRENT.

The open critical semantics, one row per unit and semantic, with the disposition the contract result gives, the cause code, the sentences that say why the semantic is open and what would close it, the instances of a repeated unit and the alarm card where there is one. These are the rows the decision records name as their members; workspace.json carries the tally of them, with the run it belongs to.

The RTO and RPO you stated (or that none was stated) and, for each unit that holds state or states a zone, replication or backup fact, what the source states. No unit is called resilient and no intent is chosen.

The resilience block of workspace.json with every unit that states a failure-domain, replication or backup fact or holds state (the quoted source facts, the state and where each fact is read from), as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to. workspace.json carries the tally of the units.

For each unit that runs as an identity or is one: the identities the source names, the static credential the knowledge base reads, the federation facts, the attachment the identity plan holds and its state. It makes no claim that federation is an option; privilege delta, break-glass access and human identity are not assessed.

The sovereignty requirement (not provided unless your applications file states one), the dimensions of sovereignty with what the source shows and what the target is proposed to be, the dependencies and the exitability. Sovereignty is not residency; it holds no score and certifies no legal compliance.
The sovereignty block of workspace.json as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to.

The price_snapshot block of workspace.json as a file of its own, with the run it belongs to: which snapshot of the public STACKIT price list this run cites (source, retrieval date, sha256, currency, net list price) and how many of the drafted resources it priced. It holds list prices only: no quantity is read, no total is built, and no usage and no egress is computed.

The cost model of the run, line by line: for each component of the source (its servers and disks) and of the STACKIT target (servers and volumes) its quantity (a value, a range or unknown, and where it comes from), its price record or the reason there is none, its pricing state and its amount; then the totals of the estate and of each service for each side (full, partial or none), the comparison of source and target with the reason a saving is or is not given, the price sources (the local price cache) and the assumptions the figures rest on. An estimate under one labelled scenario, not a bill.

One row for each line of the cost model (financial/cost-model.json), source and target: the quantity with its provenance, the price record (SKU, rate, unit, the date it is valid from, the snapshot it comes from) or the state and the reason there is none, and the amount of a priced line. An empty amount is a line that is not priced, never a zero.

The technical mapping beside the prices: for each server, boot disk, disk and database whose source and target are both in the computed group of the cost model, what each side states about vCPU, memory, CPU model, disk capacity, IOPS, throughput and high availability. The source side is read from the attributes of the source resource, the target side from the catalogue snapshot of the region; a fact a side does not state is the words not stated. A machine type is one of the types of the catalogue with at least the vCPUs and memory of the source (a burstable source may be offered shared types); a storage class is the one the draft names (the customer's answer or the variable's default), shown with the catalogue's own IOPS and throughput. The table states sizes; it is not a statement about the performance of the target against the source (no benchmark was run, and a CPU model that a side does not state is shown as not stated). The last six columns add, for a disk, the fee of the selected performance class (the cost model's own amount) with the assumption behind the class, whether the class covers the IOPS and throughput of the source volume, and the smaller classes of the catalogue that still cover them with their fee and change (an alternative with the same or better figures than the source; not a recommendation), and, for a server, whether the flavor is with or without CPU overprovisioning (the documentation's terms, by the overcommit the catalogue states) and what STACKIT states of its lifecycle (a deprecated type says so, with the sentence of the documentation). The size match columns state the comparison of a server's machine type with the source instance and of a database's PostgreSQL Flex flavor with the database instance of the source (vCPUs, memory and the kind, single node or replica set, against its high-availability setting) as proven, to review, not met or unknown, with the sentence that says what was compared; a basis names a size only where the size match is proven.

What the cost model covers: the price sources it looked at, the lines by pricing state for each side, the totals with their state (full, partial or none), the comparison of source and target and why a saving is or is not given, the assumptions, and what the list prices of the STACKIT snapshot cover, with what is known of the terms of reuse of the price data.

One row per property the draft names as not carried: the unit, the node and the property, what the assessment states about it (the class and closure of the critical-property gate, the draft's own reason, the contract semantic that reads it, what closes that semantic while it is open) and the place of the node in the source. A cell the assessment states nothing for is empty.
The units for which the draft names properties as not carried, with how many, and the units that have no count (their draft block was not accounted, or they need no resource of their own).

The reverse table of the evidence index: one entry per block of the draft, with the units it comes from, whether it is an HCL block, a comment or not placed, and its file and line, with the hop table and the checks over the draft. workspace.json carries the tally of the entries and, on each unit, the forward hops; this file is the mirror of them, with the run it belongs to.

The full comment of each block of the Terraform draft that has one: the draft keeps a one-paragraph comment above the block (where it comes from, why its values are what they are, what is not carried, which decision is open) and a `# trace: TR-...` line, and the section of this folder that line names holds the whole comment the generators wrote, unabridged: the rule and knowledge-base stamp, the references with their digests, the evidence of each chosen value and the reason of each attribute that is not written. One file for each file of the draft that has such a block, named after it with the extension .md, one section for each block under an anchor that is its trace id; the blocks are linked to their file by `trace_file` and their anchor `trace_id` in engineering/evidence-index.json. This run wrote 6 files with 10 sections.

One row per block with a trace: the trace id, the block, the draft file, the source units, the lines of the comment as the generators wrote it and the lines the draft keeps, and the pointer of the block (the trace file and the anchor of its section).

The execution package: execution/README.md is the entry point for carrying the migration out (the verdict for the resources with a typed plan and the draft files it does not cover, what is created, what is not migrated, the decisions, the credentials, the order of the steps, the OpenTofu and API commands, the manual steps, the checks and the rollback); execution/terraform/apply.md, one request file and one script per STACKIT API call under execution/api/, execution/manual/actions.md and execution/verify/checks.md beside it; execution/deploy.sh, the one entry point that carries the steps out in the order of the plan, up to the verification (no argument: a dry run that prints the order; --run: stops at each step that waits, and resumes from review/progress.yaml), with the template of the remote state (execution/backend.tf.template), one example of a pipeline (execution/ci-pipeline.example.yml) and, when a step sits between OpenTofu blocks, the generated roots of the stages before the draft (execution/stages/); a run whose plan holds checks that are commands, or a load balancer in the network of a cluster, also holds the scripts that run those checks and fill the values of the cluster, this entry names them when the run wrote them. A rendering of execution-plan.json and of the facts of the staged draft (the variables, outputs and manifests the scripts read); nothing in it has been run, and a script stops before it calls anything when its step waits for a decision. Present only when the run produced the draft. This run also wrote the scripts execution/deploy.sh, execution/verify/verify.sh.

One row per step of execution-plan.json for a spreadsheet: id, phase, mode, source, target, dependencies, owner, status, file, risks, rollback, whether it is executable and the decisions it waits for. The steps to carry out, not the register of open items (migration/actions.csv). Present only when the run produced the draft.

One row per work package of the manual steps of execution-plan.json for a spreadsheet: the steps of one phase, one owner role and one kind of work that one person carries out together, with their number, the resources they touch, the decisions they rest on and wait for, the strictest state among them, their success conditions and the ids of the steps. Every manual step is in exactly one package; execution/README.md lists the same packages. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The network and security view as a Mermaid flowchart, or, in an estate with more than 120 units in it, the partition map of the files under architecture/partitions/ (one box for each partition, the arrows between partitions counted, every unknown edge accounted for). Drawn from the TargetPlans of the draft and the assessment: the internet, public IPs, load balancers, networks, subnets, servers, databases, security groups and their rules, network ACLs and routing. A path the sources do not state is a dashed edge labelled unknown with its reason, never a connection that was not read. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The identity view as a Mermaid flowchart (an estate with more principals than a drawing keeps legible gets one sentence that names assurance/identity-transition.md, which lists every identity, instead of a drawing): the Google Cloud principal, the decision the assessment and the plan hold for it, the STACKIT identity it moves to, the role assignment and its scope. A step the typed plan does not hold (the role assignment) is drawn as manual, and a step it leaves open is a dashed edge labelled unknown. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The data flows as a Mermaid flowchart, or, in an estate with more than 120 units in it, the partition map of the files under architecture/partitions/ (one box for each partition, the arrows between partitions counted, every unknown edge accounted for): clients, load balancers, applications, databases, object storage and registries, with the protocol and port of each flow where the source states them, public or private, and the migration effect on the unit that carries it; what the source does not state is written unknown. The flows are the paths the listeners and security group rules permit, not observed traffic. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The network and security view drawn offline: the same boxes and arrows as architecture/network-security.mmd, each arrow numbered, with a key that gives its two ends in the direction of the arrow and its words (protocol, port and direction of a rule; the attribute of a reference). Source links, target links (what a rule, route or listener of the draft permits), links an answer of the inputs file changed and unknowns are drawn apart and named in the legend. A view that is not drawn whole (a partition map above 120 units) is one sentence. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The data flow view drawn offline: the same boxes and arrows as architecture/data-flows.mmd, each flow numbered, with a key that gives its two ends in the direction of the flow, its protocol and port, public or private, and the migration effect. Source links, target links and unknowns are drawn apart and named in the legend. A view that is not drawn whole (a partition map above 120 units) is one sentence. Present only when the run produced the draft.

The execution plan laid out in ten waves: wave 0 the decisions some step waits for, then the landing zone, network and security, data services, platform, workloads, data migration, cutover, verification and decommission. Each step names what it does, the Google Cloud resource, the mode, what it depends on and whether it is ready, blocked by a decision, not ready or refused. It holds the steps of execution-plan.json only. Present only when the run produced the draft.

What the STACKIT organization and project have to provide before the first apply: organization and project, network area and region, address ranges, routing, DNS, identity, service enablement, quotas to check, API access, Terraform permissions, external dependencies and the customer decisions. Read from the TargetPlans, the execution plan and the assessment; what they do not state is written as unknown and no limit or role name is invented. Present only when the run produced the draft.

Where, in this folder's files, the entries and ledger rows of each unit sit, as byte offsets: the explain command (stacktoit explain) reads a unit's chain from it without parsing the whole files. Machine-only: it is not an exchange document and states nothing the files it points into do not state; without it, or when it does not fit the files, explain reads them in full and prints the same answer.
